newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua's post-election spat will not go away.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua's post-election spat will not go away.

text.p: A nasty post-election squabble between Nicaragua's two top political parties was threatening its stability and governability, analysts said on Sunday.
Election authorities over the weekend proclaimed right-winger Arnoldo Aleman winner of the Nicaragua's Oct. 20 presidential vote, topping left-wing Sandinista leader Daniel Ortega 51 to 38 percent.
But Ortega on Sunday said that while Aleman's win was legal, he would not recognise its legitimacy since the elections were fraudulent.
"We cannot accept what was totally fraudulent ... to accept it as legitimate would be a serious error," Ortega said on the television talk show Esta Semana.
International observers have judged Nicaragua's elections flawed but fair, discounting allegations of widespread fraud.
Speaking to reporters, Ortega also rebuffed a call by Aleman to work together to rebuild Nicaragua, saying, "we are not for co-governing ... we are going to be the opposition."
Hostility between the two bitter rivals who dominate Nicaraguan politics, and the failure of the recent elections to heal the wounds, has led some analysts to fear for Nicaragua's future.

The next government "won't be able to advance any economic or social proposals if a political equilibrium is not found," warned political analyst Alejandro Serrano. "They say history repeats itself. Nicaragua is still polarised between pro-Sandinista and anti-Sandinista forces."
Meanwhile businessleaders watched nervously, wondering if Nicaragua will revert to the political squabbles and instability that have plagued its past.
Ortega, who led Nicaragua's 1979-1990 Marxist government, said the elections produced a political crisis that could deepen depending on how the incoming government behaves.
"If the new government comes at us hard, as some liberal leaders have said, they are going to polarise the country. They are going to create violence and instability," he said.
Aleman, the former right-wing mayor of Managua, is known for his fierce anti-Sandinista stance and Sandinistas fear he will try to break them as a political force once in power.

Despite losing the presidency, the Sandinistas came out of the elections a top political force, winning almost 40 percent of the seats in the National Assembly and 52 city councils. They remain the backbone of the unions, army and police.

Analysts have warned of the reaction of Sandinista activists and unions with a history of boisterous social protest, to a right-wing Aleman government they feel robbed them of the election. Aleman takes office on Jan. 10.
